name: Battery C, 62nd Coast Artillery (AA) / 62nd AAA Gun Bn

note: 1st Bn, 62nd CA (AA) became the 62nd AAA Gun Bn at Palermo; the battery's own reports switch name between Mar and Apr 1944. note: Its entry in the ETO order of battle begins etoob-28ID/p109. note: German. In December 1944 "already was deployed in the Eifel sector of the West Wall adjacent to the Our" (cole/8/p177), then at Bastogne. note: German. Followed so far by its symbols on the 12th Army Group's situation maps (records/fronts/, unit `de-3pzgr`): the map's hatched "3" with the armored mark (with or without the cross), from 21 December, where it is the day's one such symbol and not where the 3d Parachute stands; the other "3"s are `which-unit`.

note: German. Like the Fuehrer Grenadier Brigade, raised from the Grossdeutschland (cole/21/p533). name: 20th Naval Construction Battalion
plain: a naval construction battalion (Seabees), about a thousand men who built airstrips, roads and bases, followed from Nouméa through the Solomons and New Guinea to Okinawa
note: Seabees. Formed at the Naval Construction Training Center, Norfolk, August 1942. Sailed in two waves, from San Francisco on 6 Oct and from San Pedro on 29 Nov 1942 (ncbhist-020/p10-p11), and reunited at Nouméa on 13 Dec 1942. In May-June 1943 it split: a Forward Echelon of about 500 men (the 1st Section) went to Townsville, Woodlark and Kiriwina with the Seventh Fleet; the Rear Echelon (the 2nd Section; its rolls are headed "Detachment" in Sep 1943 and "Second Section" from Dec 1943) went by Guadalcanal and the Russells to New Georgia with the Third Fleet. Reunited on Banika, Russell Islands, 6 Jun 1944; home in September 1944; Saipan and Okinawa in 1945 (in two echelons, April and May); broken up there on 29 Aug 1945, its men transferred to the 15th, 36th, 79th and 126th Battalions (ncbhist-020/p2-p3; rg24-190273312/p0835). Its 1942 rolls number the sections the other way round: the roll headed "Sec 2" in Oct 1942 is the first wave, forwarded from Nouméa, while "Section 1" was still at Port Hueneme.

relations.note: The half that sailed from Port Hueneme on 6 Oct 1942 (the rolls' "Sec 2"); reunited with the second wave at Nouméa on 13 Dec 1942 (ncbhist-020/p2).
The half that stayed at Port Hueneme until 26 Nov 1942 (the rolls' "Section 1") (ncbhist-020/p2).
About 500 men: Townsville, Woodlark, Kiriwina, Milne Bay, Brisbane; the 1st Section from October 1943 (ncbhist-020/p2-p3).
The rest: Guadalcanal, the Russells, New Georgia, then Banika; the 2nd Section, its rolls headed "Detachment" and "Second Section" (ncbhist-020/p2-p3).

About 400 men (12 officers, 403 men; 1 1/2 companies) under Lt. Riordan at Oloana Bay, Vangunu (ncbhist-020/p2, p11; mcsol ch. 2). Its first echelon (3 officers, 114 men) left for Bau Island on 9 September 1943, its second (10 officers, 262 men) for Ondonga on 9 and 15 October (ncbhist-020/p11-p12). (split from Rear Echelon)

About 140 men (3 officers, 142 men; one company) under Lt. Sanders at Viru Harbor (ncbhist-020/p2, p11); left in echelons on 5-9 September 1943 for East Rovianna and Doke Doke, and from East Rovianna for Bau Island, arriving 5 November (ncbhist-020/p11-p12). (split from Rear Echelon)

The PT-boat base on Bau Island, Rendova Harbor: Group One's first echelon from 10 September 1943, joined by the Viru company on 5 November; 4 officers and 211 men left for the Russells on 9 January 1944 (ncbhist-020/p11-p12). (split from Rear Echelon)
23 officers and 749 men, Saipan to Okinawa in four LSTs, 12-17 April 1945 (ncbhist-020/p12; LST-824 and LST-898 war diaries).
4 officers and 276-277 men, on Saipan until 7 May 1945; joined the first echelon on Okinawa on 14 May (ncbhist-020/p12, p5).

name: Convoy MI-11
plain: a sixteen-ship convoy carrying Army units and other transport, Takao to Manila, attacked off north-west Luzon on 31 July 1944
note: Takao to Manila, sailing at 0500 on 29 July 1944 with sixteen ships and six escorts. The ships carried Army units and other transport (the Navy's monthly summary for July, p9). From about 0330 on the 31st (Tokyo time) submarines attacked one after another; the summary gives no position. Four ships were sunk (Yoshino, Manko, Fuso and Koei Maru: the fourth name is cursive on the July page and written plainly 光栄丸 in the 2nd Demobilization Bureau's copy of the summary, p33) and two were torpedoed and damaged (No. 1 Ogura Maru, Dakar Maru). The convoy withdrew for a time to Pangui Bay at the north-west tip of Luzon. PARCHE and STEELHEAD attacked it that night, at about 19N 121E by their own reckoning. (The 1st Surface Escort's diary has a convoy "ミ一?" attacked off Cape Bolinao, some 150 nm further south; which convoy and which night are not yet settled.)

name: Convoy TAMA-21C
plain: a twenty-ship Takao–Manila convoy that lost six ships in the Luzon Strait on 16-17 July 1944
note: TAMA-21C, a Takao–Manila convoy, appears in the 1st Surface Escort Division's July 1944 chart (別表第七) as 20 ships with the operations party (一) and seven escorts. The escorts' cell is partly legible: 海一, 海二, 草垣, 掃?三?, 前?島, 円島, 駆?六二. The Navy's summary gives the convoy as 8 escorts and 21 transports (C16120659800 p5). The convoy left Takao on the 14th. The first attack came on the morning of the 16th, and Seattle Maru sank at 1030 with 4,300 troops on board. Because of her sinking the convoy sailed in two parts, the ships rescuing her and the convoy ("沈没ノ為之ガ救助船団ト二分航行中", re-read at 500 dpi; neither part's ships are given). Before dawn on the 17th an enemy submarine that had followed the convoy sank five more ships (the narrative, p10). The chart puts the attacks between 19-17N 120-15E (16th, 0945) and 18-53N 119-44E (17th, 0345). The convoy reached Manila about the 19th. Afterwards the division ordered a meeting to study the attack and sent a staff officer to Manila.
